title: How To Respond To A Disrespectful Student
author: Michael Linsin
summary: This article outlines a nine-step protocol for handling disrespectful students without escalating the conflict or damaging the teacher-student relationship. The sequence runs from losing the battle in the moment (resisting the urge to scold or get even), staying calm and pausing silently with eye contact, ending the incident quickly, deliberately moving on and ignoring the behavior for a period, and finally enforcing a consequence - bypassing the normal warning step and going straight to time-out - once the student has mentally moved past the incident. For overt disrespect he recommends notifying parents with a letter home rather than a verbal lecture. Linsin argues that this restrained approach places the full responsibility for the behavior on the student, since the teacher never argued, retaliated, or lowered themselves to the same level, which is what makes an eventual apology sincere rather than coerced.
points: Resisting the urge to scold, argue, or "win" in the moment preserves the teacher's long-term influence.
A silent pause with sustained eye contact, followed by moving on, de-escalates the incident without a power struggle.
Overt disrespect warrants skipping the normal warning step and going directly to a consequence like time-out.
A letter home, rather than an in-person lecture, is the recommended way to notify parents of serious disrespect.
Keeping composure throughout places the full responsibility for the incident on the student, making a sincere apology more likely.
quotes: A disrespectful student can get under a teacher’s skin like almost nothing else.

When a student is disrespectful to you, you have to be willing to lose the battle. In other words, you must resist the urge to admonish, scold, lecture, get even, or otherwise attempt to put the student in their place.
In the immediate moments following the incident, don’t say a word. Simply maintain eye contact with the student and wait.
Your pause and unwillingness to react is unnerving and will leave the student devoid of anything to say. As soon as you break eye contact and walk away, the incident is over.
I recommend bypassing the warning step of your classroom management plan and sending the student directly to time-out.
For overt disrespect, the parents should be notified. A letter home is most effective. It also adds a layer of accountability that lasts beyond the day of the incident.

You didn’t yell, threaten, scold, or lower yourself to the same level of disrespect. You kept your cool and allowed accountability to work, which is the right thing to do for both you and the student.
